summary: Tiramisu is a C++-embedded polyhedral DSL whose scheduling language adds commands for partitioning loops across nodes (distribute), explicit send/receive operations and memory-hierarchy placement. A four-layer IR separates the algorithm (I), loop order and processor tags (II), affine data layout (III) and communication/synchronization (IV); distributed loops become MPI-rank conditionals and sends/receives become MPI calls. On 16 nodes it beats distributed Halide by 1.31-3.25x on image-processing kernels because the user states exactly what to send.
why_read: It is the scheduling-language polyhedral compiler in which distribution and point-to-point communication are explicit schedule commands rather than compiler-derived, the opposite design point from distributed Pluto.
main_contribution: A polyhedral scheduling language with explicit distribute, send and receive commands, implemented over a four-layer IR that keeps data layout and communication out of the loop-transformation layer.
main_limitation: Partitioning, communication and its granularity, synchrony and ordering are written by the user; the compiler only lowers them to MPI, and the distributed evaluation covers seven image kernels against one baseline.
evaluation_method: Median of 30 runs on a 16-node Xeon/Infiniband cluster (MVAPICH2) and one K40 GPU; single-node DL and linear-algebra kernels vs. Intel MKL and reference code; image-processing kernels vs. Halide and PENCIL on CPU/GPU and vs. distributed Halide on 16 nodes; strong scaling 2-16 nodes
states_relationship_to: Amarasinghe and Lam 1993, distributed-memory code generation [1]
Vocke et al., Halide for DSPs [48]
Del Sozzo et al. 2018, FPGA backend [14]
notes: CGO 2019 published version not read; card is from arXiv v5 (Dec 2018). multi-gpu-cluster rests only on Table I's 'Distributed GPU code generation: Yes' with no experiment. Tile-size autotuning (Sec. VI-A) was an external step for sgemm, not tagged. Distributed DL benchmarks: none; distributed evaluation is image processing only.
